name: Wiio's Laws
statement: Communication usually fails, except by accident.
meaning: A humorous but pointed, deliberately pessimistic take on how genuinely hard successful communication is. The joke is that mutual understanding is the exception, not the rule, when a message does land correctly, it is almost a fluke. It is the communication-theory analogue of Murphy's law: assume it will go wrong.
mechanism: The laws catalogue the many ways messages break down: ambiguity, so a message that can be read several ways is read the most damaging way; receiver-side reinterpretation, since someone always knows better than you what you meant; noise and distortion that compound as a message spreads; sender overconfidence, so contentment with your own message signals failure; and, in mass communication, the gap between how things are and how they seem. More communication does not fix this: it speeds the spread of misunderstanding.

examples.text: Both leave the same conversation certain of what was agreed, and certain they were clear, yet understanding opposite things. The fundamental law plus its corollary that apparent success hides a misunderstanding.

examples.tag: The more you say, the worse it gets
examples.text: A company-wide announcement spawns as many interpretations as it has readers: the corollary that the more we communicate, the faster misunderstandings propagate.
An email that could be sincere or sarcastic is read the more damaging way: the corollary that an ambiguous message is interpreted so as to maximise the damage.

variants.name: The corollaries
variants.text: Wiio spun out sub-laws: if communication can fail it will; if it cannot fail it still usually does; if it seems to succeed, there is a misunderstanding; if you are content with your message, it certainly fails.

variants.name: Murphy's law
variants.text: The direct model — 'anything that can go wrong will'. Wiio's laws are its communication analogue, applying the same cheerful pessimism to human understanding.

variants.name: The Shannon–Weaver model
variants.text: The serious counterpart: the formal sender–channel–noise–receiver model of communication, of which Wiio's laws are the folk parody.

whyItMatters: It is a memorable, deflating corrective to the assumption that communicating is easy or that being clear guarantees being understood. Its value is rhetorical and cautionary: it tells communicators to expect misreading, check for it, and never mistake their own satisfaction for the reader's comprehension.

working.text: treat successful communication as the exception; confirm understanding rather than presuming your message landed.

working.lead: Remove ambiguity before it is exploited
working.text: since an ambiguous message is read the most damaging way, close off the bad readings in advance.
satisfaction with your message is, by the law's own joke, a warning sign: pressure-test clarity from the receiver's side.

limits: These are humoristically formulated observations: a facetious, satirical adage, not an empirical theory. They are deliberately pessimistic and not falsifiable scientific claims; their worth is rhetorical and cautionary, reminding communicators not to assume they have been understood, rather than measured. The English wording of the corollaries is translated from Finnish, so exact phrasing varies across sources.
misreadings: It is a comic maxim, not a finding: it does not measure a real failure rate of communication, and 'usually fails' is rhetorical exaggeration in the spirit of Murphy's law. The 'modelled on Murphy's law' framing is an analogy: the resemblance is acknowledged, not a documented account of Wiio consciously copying it.
origin: Formulated by the Finnish communication scholar and politician Osmo Antero Wiio (1928–2013), a professor at the University of Helsinki and a member of the Finnish Parliament, and dated to his 1978 book on the laws. They are explicitly framed as the human-communication equivalent of Murphy's laws.
